paras: The threatened lynching at Dover, Delaware, took place on the night of July 30 or 31, 1910, when a street crowd that included white men threatened to lynch Joseph "Tough" Turner, a Black man, after a shooting among Black men on Loockerman Street, the capital's busiest thoroughfare. Two policemen got the man away from the crowd, and no lynching took place. Wire reports named Turner as the gunman, but local follow-ups described him as the man who had been shot, and another Black man, Lewis W. Davis, was held on the charge.

Dispatches from Dover said Turner had been in several earlier shooting affrays. According to the Milford Chronicle, Turner, aged 30 and living in Dover, was among a group of Black men near Dover on Saturday when a fight broke out, and he was alleged to have struck Lewis Davis on the head with a whiskey bottle. The Chronicle reported that Davis went home, armed himself with a revolver and went looking for Turner.

In the wire account, Turner got into an altercation with another Black man on the crowded street and emptied a .32-calibre revolver, wounding two Black men, one of them an old man. During the shooting and arrest, men on the street, among them what the reports called "young white athletes," dashed toward him calling to each other to "get a rope."

Policeman Hurd and an assistant held the crowd off, and the Smyrna Times wrote that any weakening on their part "would have meant a summary lynching." The Wilmington Evening Journal's wire copy said the policemen seized the man and hurried him to jail.

Turner was taken to the Delaware Hospital in Wilmington with two bullet wounds in his back and a bullet believed to be in his abdomen, and was reported in critical condition. He could not describe the shooting himself, and his sister, who went with him, gave the account. Magistrate Wood held Davis to await the result of Turner's injuries.

In mid-September Davis, described as "awaiting trial for the attempted murder of 'Tough' Turner," was one of six prisoners who broke out of the Dover jail; he was found hiding in a hog pen and returned within the hour. No arrest of anyone in the crowd is reported, and no account of Davis's trial or of Turner's recovery appears in the coverage.

The story reached readers on August 1 in two wire versions. One, under an August 1 Dover dateline, ran in the Washington Evening Star as "Policeman Saved Negro," in the Newark Evening Star as "Negro Shot Up Dover; Just Escaped Lynching" and in the Wilmington Evening Journal as "Cry 'Lynch' in Dover Streets." The other, dated July 31, ran in the New York Sun as "Negro Shoots Up Town" and two days later in the Smyrna Times as "Melee Excitement at Dover."

Both versions placed the blame on Turner and credited the police, without criticism of the crowd; the longer one said he had acted "following a new custom of some angry Delaware negroes," and the Smyrna Times called it an "attempt to shoot up a whole town." On the same day, the Evening Journal's own Dover correspondent gave a different picture, saying Davis had done "most of the gun play" and that the crowd turned when it "realized how many lives had been risked in the negroes altercation." All of the coverage found came from white newspapers; no Black newspaper is known to have carried the story.

Accounts differ on who fired: the wire reports made Turner the gunman who shot two other Black men, while the Wilmington and Milford follow-ups made him the man shot by Davis, and the September jail report described Davis as awaiting trial for Turner's attempted murder. The local reports name the accused and the magistrate and are borne out by the later jail news, but they do not say whom the crowd threatened. The wire's statement that police hurried Turner to jail also stands against reports that he lay critically wounded in a Wilmington hospital. The wire also placed the shooting on July 31, while the local papers put it on Saturday night.

framing.detail: Headlines 'Policeman Saved Negro', 'Negro Shot Up Dover; Just Escaped Lynching', 'Cry "Lynch" in Dover Streets' and 'Negro Shoots Up Town' put the danger on Turner and treat the lynch threat as a near miss averted by police.

The Smyrna Times called the shooting part of 'a new custom of some angry Delaware nergoes' and an 'attempt to shoot up a whole town', while crediting Policeman Hurd for preventing 'a summary lynching'.
The Evening Journal's own Dover special and the Milford Chronicle treated it as a shooting affray among Black men, naming Davis as the accused.
